title: Start a small repertoire from the games you actually face
outcomes: Builds a short list of replies from his own opponents' first moves, with a plan sentence for each
Reads an openings table for how often a move is played, not for what it is worth
Separates forcing lines worth remembering from flexible positions worth understanding

steps.text: A repertoire is a short list of replies to what you actually meet. Start from your own games, not from a book. Write the first three or four moves of your last ten games, as White and as Black. Count which positions repeat, and build replies for the two you meet most, one colour at a time.

steps.prompt: From your last ten games: which first moves do you most often face as Black, and which two positions come up most as White? Write them down. Which two will you prepare first, and why those?

steps.text: The Openings page of this site (route #/openings) lists, for a position, the moves players chose, how many games, and the share of wins, draws and losses. Read it for **what you will meet**. Results show how players scored, not what a move is worth. Your own games tell you which lines matter to you.

Two kinds of position. In a **forcing** line, one slip loses at once, so an exact move is worth remembering and revisiting. In a **flexible** position many moves work, so learn the plan, not the move order. Spend memory on the first kind and understanding on the second.

steps.title: Memorise or understand?
steps.prompt: In which position would remembering one exact move pay? Predict, then check.
Pick one reply you chose today. Write its plan in one sentence without naming a move. Then write one position where you would need to remember an exact move.

sources: opening data: lichess chess-openings (CC0), Lichess games (CC0); the Openings page is produced separately
